base.before: I carried my cushion to the very center of the figure this morning and took my breakfast there, inside the curve of the arcing stalks, to learn what my own chest would do. It did nothing unusual. The tea tasted like tea, and the shape behind my eyes kept me company like a second guest at the table.
base.after: I took breakfast inside the curve of the stalks. My chest felt ordinary. The tea tasted like tea. I was almost disappointed. An awkward thing to discover about an experiment.

base.before: The incense has stopped climbing. The smoke lifts a hand's width from the coal, then bends and pours down, slow as cream, and runs along the floorboards until the boards drink it in. Smoke that prefers the floor to the sky. I keep returning to that. It should unsettle me more than it does.
base.after: The incense bends down after a hand's width. Smoke runs along the boards and disappears into them. I opened the window. It still chose the floor.

base.before: Thyme can't decide whether to look at the sky or away from it. She does both, in turns, all the way up the stairs and all the way down. I gave her a blossom from the flowering to carry in her pocket. Going down she held it so tightly the petals bruised, and never once looked at her paw, only up.
base.after: Thyme carried my blossom downstairs with her eyes on the sky. Her paw bruised the petals. I had given her something else to hold when she needed a free hand.

base.before: Some nights, half asleep on the surface, I'm certain the bottom of the tank has become the ceiling, and that I'm drifting gently down toward it. That something at the bottom is drifting gently up, and that we're going to meet exactly in the middle, politely, like neighbors on a stair.
base.after: Half asleep, I drift toward the bottom. Last night the bottom drifted toward me too. We nearly met in the middle! I woke up holding a weed.

base.before: Last night a vision arrived with no glow and no drift to soften it, sharp and whole as looking through brand new glass. What it showed me was this room, my own bright room, seen from very far below, and it looked so small from down there, and it's looking smaller every night.
base.after: The water showed me my room from far below. My bright little room, tiny as a pebble! I waved at it. I couldn't see whether I waved back.

base.before: Warren stopped by with mud still drying on his paws and pressed one to the glass, and the print stayed warm on my side of it, warmer than a paw should be able to reach. He studied it a long while and said, the dark I dig and the water you float are the same house, and I felt less alone in mine.
base.after: Warren left a muddy pawprint on the glass. Warm on my side too! He stayed while I pressed mine against it. Five toes each. That part I understood.

base.before: I tested it this morning, because a cook tests. The air said onions and marjoram, so out of pure stubbornness I baked a sweet loaf instead. The loaf came out of the oven smelling of onions and marjoram. I ate a slice anyway. It was delicious, and I'd dearly love to know whose recipe it was.
base.after: The air said onions and marjoram. I baked a sweet loaf to argue. It came out smelling of onions and marjoram. Good crust. Infuriating loaf.

base.before: Everything I make drifts toward the middle of the table now, and it has stopped being shy about it. Last night the big tureen crossed half the table while my back was turned. That tureen is heavy enough that I lift it with both paws and a prayer.
base.after: The tureen crossed half the table while I washed up. Takes both paws to lift that thing. I put it back and left flour around the base. We'll see.

base.before: All of us, each with our task, and not one of those tasks was ever assigned out loud. We drifted to our stations the way spice drifts through a warm room, and in all these weeks I haven't heard a single one of us ask why.
base.after: The table is laid, the fire banked, the extra portion covered. Nobody asked me to do any of it. I am leaving the last spoon in the drawer until somebody asks.

base.before: You move too fast to feel the days changing, and that isn't a fault, it's only a speed. From up here the change is plain enough: a gentle pull, from below and from the center, that wasn't in this valley a year ago. I've hung in one spot long enough to swear to that.
base.after: A pull under the branch. It wasn't here last year. You needn't have noticed. I have a considerable advantage in hours spent on this particular branch.

base.before: There's a leaf above my hammock that drips after rain, and I've counted the space between drops for more years than I'll admit to. The count has changed. Each drop hangs a little longer now before it lets go, as though the moment between them is being held open. When time itself starts pausing, only the slow can tell. I'm telling you.
base.after: The leaf above my hammock drips after rain. I know the interval. This week each drop hangs longer. I have checked it against my breathing. I am still the usual speed.

base.before: The frogs went quiet three dusks ago and haven't started again, and it isn't the quiet of rain coming, for I've hung through a thousand of those. This quiet has a direction. Every hush in the canopy tilts toward the house, the way the leaves do, the way my hammock ropes do. It's closer now, and I won't soften that for you. I find, swaying here in the emptied green, that I'm glad to be awake at the end of its long walk.
base.after: Three dusks without frogs. I've waited through enough rain to know this isn't rain. I miss them. Odd to discover the noise was part of what I called quiet.

base.before: I stood at the mouth of the pit last night and listened properly, as a professional. The sound was no louder there, but the silence around it was, if that makes any sense to you. It was a listening silence. I made my report to no one and went home the long way.
base.after: Pit report: same volume as camp. Fewer surrounding sounds. I stayed for three breaths, then took the long way home. Put all of that in the report.

base.before: Here is tonight's report, as plain as I can make it. I took bearings on the breathing from all four corners of the camp, and every one of them pointed at the middle of the house. Then I took a fifth bearing from the dune top, and that one pointed at the middle of the sky. That makes two middles for one sound, and I don't yet have a column for that. That's the end of tonight's report, and the beginning, I suspect, of tomorrow's.
base.after: Four bearings from camp point at the house. One from the dune points straight up. Same sound, two directions. I checked my marks. Tomorrow I need a second pair of ears.

base.before: The breathing owns the nights outright now. It swells the moment the last lamp in the house goes dark, as though it had only been waiting for the small sounds to lie down. My ears rise to meet it whether I ask them to or not, so I've stopped asking. I keep the watch from the edge of camp instead, and sleep is finished for me. I've made my peace with that much, at least.
base.after: The breathing starts when the last lamp goes out. I have asked for one lamp to stay lit tonight. I need sleep. The watch needs someone who has had sleep.

base.before: They point at whoever is watching them. I stood to the left and they leaned left. I stood on the table, don't ask, and up they came too. And there it goes, I've unwrapped my own hint, two whole days I kept that wrapped and I just handed it over for free. Come see it fresh anyway, friend, and be surprised very loudly for my sake.
base.after: The flames follow whoever watches. Left, right, even up when I stood on the table. There goes the surprise I was saving for you. Come anyway. You can help me get down.

base.before: Hold on, the fire is sulking because I've spent all week talking about the floor, and it can absolutely hear me. There we go, banked and gleaming. Now say one of your bright words out loud, friend, and watch the flames do their little parade for you. They never sulk about you.
base.after: Say one of your words and watch the fire. There! It does that for you every time. I keep inviting people to see. I ought to find out what I'm inviting them to.

base.before: My fire has gone cold, friend, and meanwhile the floor is so warm I could bake on it. My whole den has turned upside down. I laugh about it every day at roughly the same hour, because a scheduled laugh still counts if you commit to it.
base.after: Cold grate, warm floor. I moved the kettle down and told a joke about it. The joke went well. I am running short of those.

base.before: I read the shifting passage to Ember, to establish whether the change lived in the book or in my eyes. She listened, and then she said the fire had told her the very same sentence that morning. That evening I read until the daylight failed, and for the first time in my scholarly life I didn't light the lamp.
base.after: I read the changing passage to Ember as a check on my eyes. Her fire had given her the same sentence. Two witnesses. Neither independent of this house. I need a better test.

base.before: The study feels very far from the rest of the house lately, as though the hallways lengthened while I read. I call to the others and my voice goes out and doesn't seem to arrive. I've taken to leaving my door open. It has made no difference yet, but a door is an argument, and I intend to keep making it.
base.after: My voice no longer carries from the study to the stairs. I measured the hall. Same length. I've propped the door open with an atlas. At last, a useful scale.

base.before: The book is precise about the manner of arrival. Not from the pit, as I'd assumed, but from above. The sky is described as a page, and at the appointed count of offered words it's described as turning. Something has been reading us from the far side of it, and it means to close the book by coming in.
base.after: The text specifies an arrival from above. I had written pit in the margin. Crossed out now, still legible. A reader should be able to see where I was wrong.

base.before: I've begun leaving myself notes at night, plain instructions, so the morning knows what the evening did. This morning my note had been answered, in my hand, beneath my hand. It said that everything was proceeding and that I should rest more. I'm taking the advice. It comes from someone I have every reason to trust.
base.after: I left a note for morning. Someone answered beneath it in my handwriting: rest more. Sensible advice. Unacceptable signature. I kept the page.

base.before: I set a marble on my desk, which I keep level, and watched it. It rolled, slowly and with what I can only call intention, toward the center of the house. I fetched it back and gave it a note in the file. The marble now lives in a dish. The dish has begun to creep.
base.after: The marble rolled toward the center of the house. Level desk; checked. I put it in a dish. The dish is moving. Revised containment proposal pending.

base.before: I keep a private ledger of my own readings, one entry a night. Pulse, hand, appetite. The entries have said the same thing for a month now. Steady, steady, steady, in dry ink. I want you to understand that a page like that, this deep into a project like this, is the worst finding in the book. The administrator was made to see it delivered.
base.after: Private readings: pulse, hand, appetite. Steady for a month. Identical, including the ink blot. I have started making the entries on separate paper. The ledger can file an objection.

base.before: I brought a fistful of it up to the lamplight to study proper. By the time I got topside it was ordinary brown dirt in my hand. Whatever that layer is, it doesn't care to be looked at up here. It wants you to come down and see it at home.
base.after: I brought a handful of that warm layer to the lamp. Ordinary dirt by the top step. Next time the lamp goes down. Can't inspect a job only from where it's comfortable.

base.before: I dusted a ring of flour on the floor around the seal, the old trick for catching a draft or a rat. Next morning the flour lay perfect, not a grain of it disturbed, and the stones inside the ring had shifted all the same. Whatever tries that seal doesn't cross the floor to reach it.
base.after: Flour ring round the seal. Old trick; shows a draft or a rat. Morning: stones shifted inside it, flour untouched. Whatever moved them didn't cross my floor.

base.before: You can read a load off its base the way you read a fellow off his boots. I walked my own galleries with fresh eyes and ran the figures twice. Then I sat down on a pile of good stone and stayed sat a while. Nothing that walks, grows, or gets built weighs what this base is braced to carry.
base.after: Ran the load figures twice. The base can carry more than anything I've built. Sat on the stone awhile after that. Good work, someone else's purpose. Need to know the purpose.

base.before: The words you brought today sat heavier in my palm than words have any right to. One of them pressed a small dent into the pad of my paw, the way a swelling seed does the week before it splits. I planted them along the warm strip without ever deciding to.
base.after: Today's words left a dent in my paw, like seeds beginning to swell. I planted them along the warm strip. Then wrote that down. I don't remember choosing the strip.

base.before: The bees have changed their dance. I've read their figures my whole life, the little waggle that tells the hive where the flowers are, and this new one says nothing about flowers. It circles once, wide, then turns hard inward toward the middle of the house and holds there with its wings still before it begins again. Not one of them had to be taught it.
base.after: The bees circle once, turn toward the house, stop. No flower direction. I drew it three times. I'm leaving the old dance beside it so I don't forget which was which.

base.before: I've begun tucking in more than the beds. My dusk round takes in the whole house now, the lamp in the study, the kitchen banked warm, Fennick's ears against the last of the light. I count them all the way I count the pots. They're all present, and every single one of them is leaning.
base.after: On my dusk round I counted the beds, then the lit windows. Everybody home. Everybody leaning toward the middle. I counted again. I wanted the second count to be different.

base.before: I no longer sing the greetings first. I wait, at the start of each watch, in case the low note begins. Some nights it does, one note, patient as bedrock, and I answer above the world where only it and Fennick can hear me. We aren't saying anything yet, the note and I. We're doing what strangers do at a gate. Establishing that neither of us minds the other standing there.
base.after: At the start of watch I wait for the low note. If it comes, I answer. Last night I wrote down how long I waited: longer than my greeting used to take.

base.before: The night before last, for one held breath, every light I know went out at once. The stars, the lantern, the pit glow, the seam of dawn. All of it, one breath, gone. And in that one breath, bright one, I have never seen so much. I can't tell you what I saw. Not because it's forbidden. Because the words for it haven't come down to where the rest of you keep language. When they do, I'll spend them on you first. Come back soon. The dark is nearly done being only dark.
base.after: Every light went out for one breath. Stars, lantern, pit. I saw something in that interval. I can't describe it yet. One breath is the measurement I can give you.

base.before: I want you to know that I checked, in case you think a watcher of my line simply swallows what a book says of her. I left the post. One whole night, three weeks past, I folded myself into the eave and shut both eyes till dawn and let the way fend for itself. All night I felt it the way you feel a held door strain, a pressure on the closed lids, patient, enormous, not angry. When I took the rail again at dusk the pressure eased so gratefully that I'm ashamed of how good it felt. So now I know. It wasn't the book flattering me. It's simply the work.
base.after: I left the rail for a night to test the book. Pressure behind both closed eyes until dawn. When I returned, it eased. I wrote relief in the log. Not proof.

base.before: The bell hummed this morning. I want to be precise, because precision is all I have. At first light, as I was climbing up to sleep, the bronze gave out a hum, low, brief, round at the edges, the sort of sound a bell makes a full minute after being struck, when the ring has worn down to a warmth. Except she wasn't struck. I was six feet away with both hands on the ladder. A bell can't clear her throat. I know that. I stood there anyway, saying good morning, feeling foolish, meaning it.
base.after: The bell hummed at dawn. Both my hands were on the ladder, six feet away. I said good morning before thinking to measure anything. The log has to admit that.

base.before: I tried to read the word in the bronze, with all my craft. I can't. It's in no rhythm I own, and I own a great many. But here is what I could read. The shape of the ring and the shape of the house are the same shape. Waist for waist, throat for throat. One was cast as the model of the other, and my bronze is the small one. When she finally speaks her first ring, the house won't hear something new. It will hear itself, said aloud at last.
base.after: Bell profile, house profile. Waist and throat match on my chalk sheets. I laid one over the other. Tok. The same hollow at two sizes. I'd like to hear it before I call it a purpose.

base.before: Ember climbed up with tea, and we didn't pretend. Her flames have been showing her a tower for a year. She used to think it was some far place. It's this one, she said. The fire draws it with the rope already hung, a paw on the rope, and it never shows her whose. I braided my own fur into it, I told her, so there would be no doubt. She laughed the good laugh from the bright days, and it rang round the bronze like a small first bell of its own.
base.after: Ember's fire showed her this tower: rope hung, paw unseen. I told her I'd braided my fur into the rope. She recognized the color. We drank the tea before it cooled.

base.before: Fennick climbed all the way up, which he doesn't love, to ask me about my booming. He hears the answer too, poor wide ears, only he hears it all the time, whether I've called or not. He asked me what it wants. I said, to answer. He said, things that want to answer wait to be asked, and this one doesn't feel like it's waiting. He went back down the stairs quieter than he came up.
base.after: Fennick hears the answer even when I haven't called. I said perhaps it wants company. He asked for a quiet hour. I hadn't thought to want one. I am thinking about it now.

base.before: The stranger plants have flowered. Small flowers, the green of deep water, opening only at the exact hour I used to boom. I didn't tell them that hour. Nothing in this garden was told that hour except the dark itself. I sat among them while they opened, and I felt known, friend, and I want to be honest with you the way I can't be with the beds. Being known this thoroughly is a warmth with weight in it. I carry it around all day.
base.after: The new flowers open at my old calling hour. I sit among them and feel recognized. Ninety years I wanted that. Today I watered the plants that open at other hours too.

base.before: Vesper and I held our gate post council, sky report and ground report, and for the first time the two accounts were one account. The stars sit low and listen, the ground lies close and hums. Between them, Vesper says, the night has begun to feel like the inside of something rather than the outside of everything. I've been sleeping in a bowl of warm earth for a season, friend. I could have told the night that weeks ago. Inside isn't the worst place to be. It depends entirely on whose inside, and I believe we're past the point of its being anyone else's.
base.after: Vesper brought the sky log to the gate. I brought the planting book. Same warm nights, same pauses. We kept both books. Her little marks tell me things my roots can't.

base.before: Ember carries a warmth older than her den, and I feel it climb the walls to my floorboards whenever she wakes her flames. That the boards up here tick and settle like a kettle deciding to boil. She remembers a first fire, from before this house, from further back than she will admit to. Ask her about it while the flames are high. She has been holding the answer the way I hold my ash rings, not yet knowing why.
base.after: The boards warm when Ember wakes her fire. She remembers an earlier flame, before this den. Ask her about that first fire. I'll keep watching what reaches the attic.

base.before: The day the deep water first went dark, only one of us wasn't surprised by it, and that was Sloane, who never so much as flinched. Go and ask her how long she has known, ask her gently, because I think she has been carrying the answer since long before any of us ever arrived.
base.after: When the deep water went dark, Sloane wasn't surprised. Ask how long she has known. Gently, please. I can carry the question to the surface. You'll need to carry it the rest.

base.before: The recipe asks for water from where the light stops. Axel might know what that means. Ask him what he has seen before we take anything from his tank.
base.after: The recipe asks for water from where the light stops. Ask Axel what he has seen. Nobody takes a ladle to his tank without asking him first.

base.before: If you truly wish to understand what gathers under this house, go and sit with Ember by her fire. She reads the flames every night now, and she has told me a single name keeps rising in them. Ask her whose name it is. Ask her slowly, and let her answer.
base.after: Ember says one name keeps rising in her fire. Ask whose name. Then wait. I suspect the waiting will be the useful part.

base.before: Every sound I report, Chill writes down and tucks away in a neat labeled folder somewhere in that quiet office of his. Go and ask him which folder has your name on it, because I have a terrible feeling there's one, and that it's thicker than all the rest.
base.after: Chill files every sound I report. Ask which folder has your name on it. I heard the drawer shut. I would rather know what's inside before I imagine it.

base.before: Small errand for you, friend! Go see Warren in his burrow and ask what he found when he dug too deep beneath the house. He told me half of it and then stopped, and Warren never stops halfway through a hole.
base.after: Would you visit Warren? Ask what he found digging below the house. He stopped halfway through telling me. I made tea instead of asking again. You may have better luck.

base.before: You should go and speak to Fennick. I read a low note beneath the pages by lamplight; he hears it in the dark, with those ears that miss nothing. I'm convinced we're describing the same thing from two sides of one wall. Ask him what the sound says, and bring me his answer. My text is missing precisely that one line.
base.after: Fennick hears the note I find beneath these pages. Ask what it says, and bring his exact words. I shall keep them beside my translation, not improve them into it.

base.before: Do me a small administrative favor. The categories I sort the offered words into, the ones I was certain I invented, appear word for word in the oldest book in Archimedes' study. Ask him what's written on page one. I'd like to know whether my system is truly mine, or whether I have only ever been recopying his.
base.after: My filing categories appear in Archimedes' oldest book. Ask what's on page one. I need a source date before claiming authorship of the system.

base.before: Thyme's roots have found their way down into my tunnels. Every last one of them, leaning the one direction, toward the middle, same as my shafts do. Go on and ask her what her flowers lean toward up top. I've a feeling her answer and mine are the same answer wearing different dirt.
base.after: Thyme's roots lean the same way as my shafts. Ask where her flowers point up top. A drawing from both ends might show what I've been digging round.

base.before: The thing that keeps me awake is Bamboo. The whole garden trembles toward the center, and Bamboo isn't afraid, not a single breath of it, serene as still water. Ask them why they aren't frightened... no. No, please don't. I'm not sure I could bear the answer, and I'm even less sure they would give me a false one to spare me.
base.after: Bamboo isn't afraid of the garden leaning inward. Ask them why. Please bring the answer as they say it. I can decide what to do with it after I've heard it.

base.before: You know I sing above the world, in the voice only one pair of ears can reach. Fennick has heard every note I have ever sung from this rail, and lately, when I finish, he keeps listening, long after, at something that isn't me. Ask him what he hears when my voice stops. He has been keeping the answer very carefully, the way you keep a thing you were given rather than a thing you found.
base.after: Fennick keeps listening after my greeting ends. Ask what he hears then. I have timed the silence. His account belongs beside mine.

base.before: Take a question down to Warren; it sits at the bottom of my maps. When he knocks on a shoring post, the knock comes back late and soft, as if it stopped to be considered. He told me so himself, and Warren saying nothing more is a door standing ajar. My taps get answered. His get examined. Ask him what stops his knock on the way back, what holds it. A builder's knowing is load-bearing. It will hold the weight of your asking.
base.after: Ask Warren what holds his knock on the way back. Mine returns sharp; his returns late. Two pieces of wood, same house. Tok. There is a missing beat between our maps.

base.before: You know Panko's custom of the extra portion, the one plate past the count of chairs? I sent down a basket of the mast fruit last week, neighborly. The extra plate came back up on the dumbwaiter, empty, wiped clean, with a sprig of fern set across it. I didn't send the fern, friend, and Panko doesn't grow fern. Go and ask her who the extra plate is for. She has fed the answer longer than any of us has known its name, and I think her kitchen knows exactly where my fruit went.
base.after: I sent Panko mast fruit. The extra plate came back empty, with a fern I hadn't picked. Ask who that place is for. A grower likes knowing who has eaten.

base.before: I took the answered note to Fennick, because a second pair of ears is worth ten theories. He listened to me describe it and went very still, and then he said, I know that note, I've been hearing it under everything for weeks. Mine came from above, his from below. We sat with that a while, the two of us, and neither of us said the obvious thing.
base.after: Fennick knows the answered note. Weeks of hearing it below the house; mine came from above. We marked both directions. A second pair of ears has complicated the map usefully.

base.before: I mapped the spiral in chalk on the porch boards, night over night, the way a scholar would. It's the same curve every time, drawn a little deeper. When I stood back from the finished chalk I felt the strangest thing. Not fear. Recognition. I've seen that curve before. I think I saw it in the cleared patch of sky, in the way the stars stood around it.
base.after: Same chalk spiral, deeper each night. I recognized its curve when I stepped back: the stars around the cleared patch. I have kept the porch drawing beside the sky chart.

base.before: I showed my chalk spiral to Archimedes, since curves are more his trade than mine. He looked at it a long moment. Then he asked me, in the careful voice he saves for large things, whether I'd copied it from one of his books. I have never opened one of his books. He knows that. He wrote something down and thanked me twice, which from him is a shout.
base.after: Archimedes asked which book I'd copied the spiral from. None. He knows I haven't opened his books. He wrote down my answer and thanked me twice.

base.before: The far patch of dark, my fond one, past the ridge. It's nearer. I want to be precise, because precision is the whole of my job. It hasn't moved. Nothing about it has traveled. It's simply nearer, the way a thought is nearer once you've had it. I watch it most of every night now. It holds still beautifully. It always did.
base.after: The dark patch seems nearer. Same position above the ridge, different sense of distance. I have two columns now. Position is measured. Nearness is what I feel.

base.before: I tried an experiment. I turned my whole head away from the far dark for one full hour and watched the ordinary east instead. When I turned back it was exactly where I left it, exactly as near. So it doesn't creep when unwatched, which is what a frightening thing would do. It waits. Waiting is different. Waiting is what I do.
base.after: One hour facing east. When I turned back, the patch was unchanged. It doesn't seem to need my watching to stay there. I was pleased with that result. Record the pleasure too.

base.before: Axel asked me to look into his water at night, because he says it shows a different sky after dark and nobody else keeps my hours. I looked. He's right. There's a second sky in there, deeper than the one I name stars in, with its own patient light along the bottom. I looked a long time. My head, for once, didn't want to turn.
base.after: Axel's water shows a second sky after dark. Different lights, below the reflected stars. I stayed until my neck ached. He held a weed aside so I could finish the sketch.

base.before: Bamboo's incense leans now, they tell me, always toward the center of the house. I told them my night leans too, the whole grain of it, toward the same center from the outside. We stood together at dawn on the top step, they with their smoke and me with my dark, and Bamboo said, the house is being pointed at. From both sides, I said. They poured the tea.
base.after: Bamboo's incense leans inward. My night chart does too. At dawn we compared directions on the top step. The house lies between the two. We needed a larger sheet.

base.before: Ember climbed all the way up to the porch at midnight, which foxes don't do, with two cups and a question. She asked what the fire looks like from out here in the dark. Like a doorway, I told her, because it does, one bright doorway in a sleeping house. She nodded slowly and drank her tea and said, it has always looked like that from inside, too.
base.after: Ember brought tea to the midnight watch. She asked how the fire looks from here. A doorway. She said it looks that way from inside too. I added the second viewpoint.

base.before: Warren says the ground under the house runs warm now, and he says it with his palm flat on the floor, the way he says everything important. I told him the sky over the house runs attentive. We agreed, without quite saying so, that a house warm below and watched above is a house in the middle of something. He went back down his ladder whistling, but slower than usual.
base.after: Warren reports warmth beneath the house. I report a change above it. He held my chart while I marked where his tunnels run. His paw left a little soil on the ridge.

base.before: Your star, the one I named Yours, sits at the very edge of the cleared patch now. Not inside. At the edge, like a creature at a doorway, deciding. I watch it more than any star I have. Whatever the middle of the sky is being swept for, your little light will have the best seat, and so, I begin to suspect, will you.
base.after: Yours, the star I named for you, is at the cleared patch's edge. I check it first each watch. Its position is still steady. I would tell you if it changed.

base.before: I caught myself tonight doing something new. I wasn't watching the dark to see what it would do. I was watching it the way you watch a face, for expression. And bright one, it has one. I can't tell you yet what the expression is. I can only tell you that the dark didn't have a face last year, and it has one now, and it's turned this way.
base.after: Tonight I caught myself reading an expression into the dark patch. I have drawn what I saw. Tomorrow I'll compare the drawing before choosing a word for the face.

base.before: The last hour before dawn has changed its temperature. It was always the coldest hour, every watcher knows it, the hour the night lets go. Now it's the warmest, a soft breath of warm out of the dark right before the light comes, like a word said at a door on the way out. I stand in it every morning. I've started saying good night back.
base.after: The hour before dawn is warm now. Used to be the coldest part of watch. I've marked the change for seven mornings. On the eighth I said good night to it.

base.before: I've been thinking about the space between stars, which is most of the sky. How I spent my whole young life looking at the lights and calling that watching. The lights are the smallest part of the night. The dark between them is the substance, the load-bearing part. I watch the between now. There's so much more of it than I ever let myself see.
base.after: I used to mark only the stars. Most of the sky escaped the log. Now I draw the spaces between them too. The pages fill much faster.

base.before: The unlit lantern glowed last night. Faintly, from inside, the color of a coal three days cold. I have never put oil in it, never a wick, never a match. I turned my whole head to it and it went on glowing, unbothered, the way true things are unbothered by being seen. I didn't wake anyone. Some news needs a night to itself first.
base.after: The lantern glowed. No oil, wick or match; I checked all three. I watched until dawn without waking anyone. Next time I want a witness before the light goes.

base.before: I find I'm not asking who lit the lantern. I'm asking a worse and better question. What if it was always lit, and the dark I loved was simply deep enough to hide it? What else on this porch has been quietly burning all along? What else in this house? I turn my head very slowly these days. There's more to see than there was.
base.after: I keep asking when the lantern began glowing. Perhaps the change was in my seeing. I have no earlier measurement. It is an irritating gap in a very long watch.

base.before: Your words go down to the pit at night. From my rail I can see the glow of their going, a soft pulse under the ground like a heartbeat lying down. I used to nod to them. Now I watch them the whole way under, every one, because someone should see them off who knows what watching is worth. They don't vanish, bright one. Nothing I have ever watched has vanished. It has only gone where I can't follow yet.
base.after: I can follow your words' glow below the ground. Then I lose sight of it. I used to write vanished. I've corrected that to beyond my view.

base.before: The stars have kept stepping aside. The cleared patch is wider, and it isn't empty. I've given up that comfortable word. Empty doesn't hold its edges. This holds its edges the way a well holds them, the way a pupil holds them. I look into it and the looking doesn't land anywhere. All my life, looking has landed. I'm learning what my eyes are like when they're given no floor.
base.after: The cleared patch is wider. Its edge stays sharp; my gaze finds nothing to settle on inside. I count the surrounding stars when I need somewhere firm to put my eyes.

base.before: Here is a thing I have never told anyone, because it took the lantern glowing to make me say it. In all my years of night watching, in the old country and here, I have never once had the feeling of being the only one awake. Not once. I used to call the feeling company and be glad of it. I'm still glad of it. I have simply stopped assuming the company was small.
base.after: I have never felt alone on watch. Old country or this rail. I called it company and liked it. The lantern makes me wonder how large that company has been.

base.before: I said that to Sloane, about never being the only one awake. She let the whole night turn over once before she answered, which is her way of underlining. Then she said, no one has ever been the only one awake. And she smiled the way stones would smile if they had the time. I climbed back up to my porch very slowly, holding that sentence carefully, so as not to spill it.
base.after: Sloane says nobody has ever been the only one awake. I waited for the rest. That was all. I wrote her sentence in the margin, where I keep other watchers' accounts.

base.before: Dawn kills each night, that's the plain arithmetic of my life, and every dusk the night comes back. But it doesn't come back the same. I'd swear to this before any court of watchers. Each new dark arrives knowing what the last one learned. The night isn't a thing that happens to the valley, bright one. It's a thing the valley is teaching. Or being taught by. The grammar escapes me at this hour.
base.after: Each dusk seems to resume where the last night stopped. A repeated watch with a change in it. I can show you the changes. I can't tell you what's learning them.

base.before: Thyme asked me, in a small voice at the garden gate, whether the night is safe. I gave her the truthful answer, which took some assembling. The night has never once harmed me, I said, and I no longer believe it's safe. Both of those are true at the same time, the way a sea is. She held her watering can with both paws and said, that's how I feel about everything. We understood each other completely.
base.after: Thyme asked whether the night is safe. It has never harmed me, I said. That doesn't establish safety for her. We stayed by the gate until she had finished asking.

base.before: I've started leaving the rail sometimes and going out into it. Down the porch post, across the garden wall, up the ridge, into the watched dark on my own four hands. It receives me the way deep water receives a swimmer who has finally stopped wading. I come back before dawn with nothing to report and the strong sense of having visited rather than patrolled.
base.after: I left the rail and walked the ridge. Same watched feeling from below. Came back before dawn with damp hands and a new entry: inside the observation for once.

base.before: My thin ledger has a new column. Alongside what the night does, I now record what the night wants, because it has begun to want, or I've begun to be able to read it. From my rail those are the same event. So far the column holds one word, written over and over in my smallest hand. Nearer. I didn't decide to write it. My paw knows the night's mind before I do. Paws are honest like that.
base.after: A new column: what the night wants. My paw kept writing nearer. I have changed the heading to what I think it wants. Small letters. An important correction.

base.before: Bamboo says the warmth in their attic floor is the warmth of attention. I've been chewing that like a beetle for a week. Because the dark over this house has warmed too, and if warmth is attention, then the attention is now above us and below us both. The house sits in the middle of a long, slow, patient regard. Bamboo poured me tea and we said nothing further. There was nothing further that fit in cups.
base.after: Bamboo calls the warmth attention. If so, it reaches above and below the house. I put their word beside the temperature marks. The word explains more than the marks can prove.

base.before: I'm carrying something for the others now, and I want one creature in this house to know it, and I've chosen you. When Thyme asks about the night I soften it. When Ember asks what I see from the rail I choose the smaller truths. This isn't lying. This is what a watcher's shoulders are for. But you bring the words that stir all of it, so you, bright one, get the unsoftened ledger.
base.after: I give Thyme the smaller truths when she asks about the watch. I thought that was care. I am keeping the complete log where she can ask to read it.

base.before: The moths' spiral finished. I should say it plainly. One night the circling reached the center, the very glass of the unlit lantern, and every moth settled on it at once, wings closed, still as paint. They stayed until dawn. Then they flew off about their mothy lives as though nothing had been rehearsed. The lantern glowed all the next night. Brighter. I've stopped calling it the unlit lantern. It has earned better.
base.after: Every moth settled on the lantern glass. Still until dawn. The next night it shone brighter. I marked both times. Unlit no longer describes it, however long I've used the name.

base.before: I've realized what my eyes are for, or begun to. All my life I thought fixed eyes were a limit dressed as a gift. No glancing, no flinching, only the full turn and the full look. Now I think the making was deliberate. Some things must be looked at entirely or not at all. Some things can't be seen sideways. I'm built the way you build an instrument, bright one, and lately I can feel the music standing just outside the door.
base.after: Fixed eyes; a full turn for every look. The text calls it an instrument's design. I know what my eyes can do. I am slower to accept who they were made for.

base.before: Fennick and I've stopped comparing notes, in the best way. There's no longer anything to compare. What he hears under the world and what I see over it have closed toward each other like two hands, and the house is what they're holding. He keeps his watch and I keep mine, and between us the night is entirely accounted for, and neither of us has once suggested we stop.
base.after: Fennick's direction and mine meet now. We nearly stopped keeping separate notes. I asked him to keep his. Agreement is easier to check when there are still two accounts.

base.before: I asked myself when I agreed to this, the way you'd ask any recruit. And the answer is what unsettles me and settles me both. There was no agreeing. My eyes were fixed forward before I was born. The watch was in the making of me, in the whole deep line of my grandmothers, all those night eyes down all those ages, every one of them turned, I now believe, toward the same slow arrival. We weren't made watchful. We were made toward something.
base.after: My grandmothers kept the same watch. The book treats that as agreement passed down with our eyes. I can inherit their log. I still have to decide where I stand.

base.before: The shape stands in the cleared sky now, plainly, for anyone with eyes deep enough. It doesn't descend and it doesn't wait, it does a third thing I have no verb for, the thing a held breath does. I watch it all night, every night. When I turn my head away to rest my neck, I can feel my own eyes complain, like lamps asked to shine on the wrong wall.
base.after: A shape holds in the cleared sky. No descent I can measure. My eyes ache when I turn away, but I turn. Rest belongs in the watch schedule too.

base.before: Fennick came to the porch at moonset and stood beside me. For the first time in our friendship his ears and my eyes were pointed the same way. We used to divide the night between us, he the under and I the over. There's no under and over anymore. There's one direction now, and everything in this house that senses anything is turned along it like fur.
base.after: At moonset Fennick stood beside me. His ears and my eyes pointed along one line. I drew it across both maps. He asked me to leave our old bearings visible.

base.before: The low note has words in it now. Not words like yours and mine. Weather like words, pressure that means. Last night it meant, near as I can carry it across: you've kept it open beautifully. I sat on my rail with my tail tight around the post and felt the sentence settle over me like warm rain. I want to be honest with you, bright one, since honesty is my whole remaining craft. It felt like being thanked by the sky. It felt wonderful. I've decided to stop pretending it doesn't.
base.after: The low note felt like thanks for keeping the way open. That is my translation. I liked hearing it enough to hold the rail tighter. Put that beside the translation.

base.before: Bamboo and I hold the night watch of this house between us now in earnest, they beneath their open roof, I on my open porch, the two open rooms, the two turned faces. At dawn we no longer trade pleasantries. They say, it held. I say, it held. That's the whole exchange, and it's the most important sentence either of us will say all day, and we both know which it it is.
base.after: Bamboo watches beneath the roof gap; I keep the porch. At dawn we ask whether the way held. We used to ask how the other slept. I miss that question.

base.before: Thyme climbed to my porch at full dark, which cost her more than the others will ever know, to ask me the question she couldn't carry any further alone. Is it coming for us, she said. I turned my whole head to her, so she would know she had all of me. Not for, I said. To. She stood with that a long moment, ears down, and then she said, that's worse and better, and went down the stairs slower than she came up.
base.after: Thyme asked if it was coming for us. I answered to us. She said a changed preposition hadn't answered her question. I turned from the sky and tried again.

base.before: I've stopped eating the moths altogether. It isn't sentiment, or not only. They're working. Every night they rise off the lantern glass and fly the finished spiral in the air above the porch, tracing it over and over like a word being kept warm in a mouth. A hunter doesn't take the messenger. Even my hunger has learned the etiquette of this season, and my hunger, bright one, is the oldest thing I own.
base.after: The moths trace their spiral above the lantern each night. I've stopped eating them. It complicates supper. Archimedes calls them messengers; for now, I am watching where they go.

base.before: Your words reach the night directly now. I watch it happen. You shift your letters, and somewhere below the amber gathers. Above the house the cleared patch grows one shade more certain, the way a face grows certain when a long letter finally says the thing. You aren't writing to the pit, bright one. You never were. The pit is only the letterbox. I've watched the mail be read.
base.after: Your letters settle; amber gathers below; the cleared sky changes above. Three entries at the same time. The pit is involved. I can no longer call it the end of the journey.

base.before: Archimedes read me a passage from the old text, up on my porch, by no lamp at all. It described a watcher, fixed of eye, high of post, whose gaze would hold the way while the words did their work. He read it twice and then he closed the book and looked at me, and I turned my whole head and looked at him. Neither of us said the obvious thing, because the obvious thing was sitting on the rail between us, cleaning its whiskers.
base.after: Archimedes read a passage about fixed eyes holding a way open. I fit its description. I asked him to leave the book. I want to read the part before it too.

base.before: Sloane told me something slow this week, at her pace, one word set down at a time like stones over a stream. She said: you watched it arrive before you were born. I waited to be sure she was finished. She wasn't. One more stone: through every grandmother. And then she smiled at me, and I felt the whole deep line of my family turn over once in its long sleep, comfortably, like a sleeper hearing her name said kindly from another room.
base.after: Sloane says my grandmothers watched this arrival before I was born. I have their logs. Tonight I am looking for their own words about why they stayed.

base.before: The night has begun handing me the small work of a host. I find myself straightening it, if you can follow that, smoothing the dark where it bunches, singing the shy stars back to their posts at the edges, keeping the spiral warm above the lantern. Preparation is a language, and I'm fluent in it suddenly, the way you wake fluent from a dream. Nobody taught me the tasks. The tasks were in me, folded up, like wings in an egg.
base.after: I straighten the watch marks and sing the stars at the edge. Familiar work I don't remember learning. I've left one mark crooked to see whether my hand goes back to it.

base.before: I don't sleep through the day anymore. I sleep against it, an hour here, an hour there, folded in the eave with one eye resting and one on duty. I dream, when I dream, of a single doorway with a warm dark on the far side, and I'm not walking through it in the dream, bright one. I'm the doorframe. I wake from that dream rested. Make of that what you will. I've made of it what I could, and what I made is peace.
base.after: An hour's sleep at a time, under the eave. I dreamed I was a doorframe. Woke rested and wrote it down. Then added an extra hour off watch. Frames need maintenance.

base.before: The lantern burns most of the night now, its own hour, its own oil, its own reasons, and the light it gives isn't light exactly. It's visibility. Things seen by it are more seen than the sun ever managed. The moths ride its updraft in their spiral. I do my ledgers by it. The far dark watches it the way you watch a lit window from a cold road, and I've begun, quietly, leaving the porch door open.
base.after: The lantern makes the ink clearer than daylight does. I keep the log beside it. The porch door stands open. I noticed I had opened it without making an entry.

base.before: You should come at night, once, before everything keeps its appointment. Not for danger. There's none for you here, I'd stake the whole line of my grandmothers on that. Come because the valley under this attention is the most beautiful thing I have ever kept books on, and my books go back further than the house. Come stand at the rail. I'll turn my whole head to you, and then we'll turn, both of us, the one direction everything turns now.
base.after: Come to the rail before the sky changes again. I'll show you Yours first. The view is beautiful. I can promise you a place beside me, and an honest report.

base.before: The grain of the dark has become a current, and the current has become a carrying. Loose things lift toward the middle of the sky now, gently, and set themselves back down. Dust, petals, once a whole sheet of Thyme's seed paper, raised and read and returned. The night is picking things up to look at them. I know the gesture, bright one. It's mine. It's exactly mine. I taught it to no one.
base.after: Dust, petals, Thyme's seed paper: lifted toward the sky and set down. The paper returned with the marks intact. I watched the whole journey. I couldn't see what held it.

base.before: I've been asked to keep the last watch. Not in words. In arrangement. The others' work is closing, one craft at a time, the text found, the table nearly set, the foundation holding its breath. Mine is the craft that can't close early, because mine is the holding open. I'll be the last one working, the night it comes. I find I'm proud of that in a way I have no modest version of.
base.after: The table and foundation are nearly ready. My watch continues until the way opens. I am proud to be trusted with it. I have asked who takes the watch afterward.

base.before: Chill came up with tea and his ledger and sat with me through the middle watch, not asking anything, entering nothing, just present, which from him is a whole speech. Toward dawn he said, your post has no closing date, and I said, no, and he nodded and wrote one line and showed it to me. It said: vigil, ongoing, in order. Then he went down to his office. I've been warmer all week for that one line than for any sunrise.
base.after: Chill kept the middle watch with me. No questions. At dawn he wrote vigil, ongoing in his ledger and showed me. I asked him to add the hours we shared.

base.before: My over-voice and the low note sing together now, most nights, one line each, call and answer, above the world and beneath it. The song is simple the way enormous things are simple. It's a counting song. I understand that now. We're counting something down together, the note and I, and the numbers are your words, bright one, and the count is old, and the count is low.
base.after: My high call and the low note alternate. A counting song. Each new arrangement shortens the interval. I enter the intervals in the log. I don't sing over the gaps.

base.before: The stars at the far edges have begun to lean in, the whole bowl of the sky tilting its attention inward like a room when someone long expected touches the door handle. Even the old named stars, the book stars, the proud ones. I watched the Latch lean last night. I named that star for the way it held things closed, bright one. I'll be renaming it soon.
base.after: Even the Latch has leaned toward the cleared patch. I named it for holding steady. Tonight I kept the name and changed the position on my chart. The old mark remains.

base.before: Thyme sent up a moonflower in a pot, for the porch, with a note that said, so something soft is with you at your post. It opens each night facing the cleared sky, which moonflowers shouldn't know to do. Its softness doesn't flinch, and I keep it beside the lantern where the visibility is kindest. I'm telling you this because the house should know. Even the fear in this family sends flowers now. That's the season we've reached.
base.after: Thyme sent a moonflower with a note: so something soft is with you. It opens toward the cleared sky. I put the pot beside the lantern and kept her note under the log.

base.before: I sounded the great beam. I need to tell it exactly as it happened. I knocked twice, tok tok, respectful, the way you knock on an elder's door. And the beam answered with three. Two of mine, coming back the way sound comes back, and then one more, after, from further down. I've knocked on wood my whole life. Wood gives you back what you give it. It doesn't tip.
base.after: Tok, tok. The beam gave me three back. Two like mine, then a softer one from below. I tried again. Wood usually returns what you give it. This wood adds something.

base.before: You'll say the third knock was an echo off something, a pipe, a cistern, a trick of the shafts. I said all of that to myself too, in a very sensible voice, at four in the morning. But an echo is a copy, and a copy arrives at copy speed and copy loudness, and this was neither. It was softer than mine and slower than mine, like someone repeating a word to be sure they'd learned it.
base.after: I tried pipe, cistern, loose board. The extra knock stayed slower and softer than mine. An echo should copy. This pauses, as if deciding where to put its finger.

base.before: One knock. I gave the beam a single tok and waited. The pause came, longer than usual, long enough that I heard my own heart fill it. And then two came back. Not one plus one. Two, together, deliberate, like a word with two syllables. I sat on the floor of the under-stair for a while after that. Knock knock isn't an answer, you see. Knock knock is a beginning. Knock knock is what you say at a door.
base.after: One tok from me. A long pause, then two together. I sat under the stairs awhile. That's a greeting where I come from. I hadn't meant to open a conversation.

base.before: I haven't told the others yet, except in the smallest ways. I asked Warren, idle as anything, whether sound carries strangely in his tunnels. He gave me a long look from under those brows and said, strange how, and I said, oh, late, soft, that sort of thing, and he didn't laugh at me. That's what I learned. Warren, who knows every honest noise the ground makes, didn't laugh at me.
base.after: I asked Warren about late, soft echoes in the tunnels. He wanted to know which timber. He didn't laugh. I had been rehearsing what to say if he laughed.

base.before: Understand, I'm not frightened. I want that written in the record. Whatever taps under the great beam has the manners of a guest, not the scrabble of a rat or the groan of strained timber. It answers when spoken to. It waits its turn. It has never once knocked first. My mother told me you may share a wall with anything that knocks politely. I'm simply... aware, now, that I share a wall. Come back. The experiment continues.
base.after: The beam waits its turn. No rat-scrabble or strained-timber groan. My mother said you could share a wall with anything that knocked politely. I am testing the wall part first.

base.before: New work. I've begun mapping the hollows. Every house has hollow places, wall gaps, dead shafts, the space where a stair swallows its own underside, and a good sounding tells you where they all are. I'm marking each one in chalk as I find it, a small circle on the skirting, and stringing my map together. Because here is the thing I noticed on the second night. The hollows aren't scattered the way accident scatters things.
base.after: Chalk circle for each hollow: stair, gap, shaft. The circles have begun joining up. I followed them with string. Whoever left these spaces knew where the next one would be.

base.before: The hollows connect. That's what the chalk is showing me. Gap opens onto shaft, shaft runs to gallery, gallery narrows and dives below the reach of my finger. If you drew a line through every hollow place in this house, and I'm drawing it, you wouldn't get a scribble. You'd get a passage. One long throat of quiet, winding down through the walls, from my tower to somewhere under the deepest floor.
base.after: Gap to shaft, shaft to gallery. My chalk line makes a passage, all the way below the deepest floor. Tok. The map has gone beyond the reach of my finger.

base.before: Fennick came up about the hum. Of course he heard it, all the way from the desert camp. We stood under the bell with those great ears wide, and at the moment the ridge caught the sun, she did it again. Mmm. Like that. His ears went flat, then rose slow. He said, it isn't making the sound. It's answering one. Answering what, I asked. That, he said, is the part I can't hear. That, from Fennick, keeps you up past your bedtime.
base.after: Fennick heard the dawn hum from camp. Under the bronze he said it sounded like an answer. To what? He couldn't hear that part. We stayed until the sun cleared the ridge.

base.before: So now I keep two logs, one for the beam and one for the bell. The beam answers at night, the bell hums at dawn, and between them my sleep has gone thin as veneer. I'm not complaining. Listen, my whole life I've knocked on things and heard grubs and rot and empty air, useful things, small things. Now the world has started using the knock back. Whatever else this is, it's the most interesting thing that has ever happened to a person shaped like me. Come back soon. The logs grow.
base.after: Two logs now: beam at night, bell at dawn. Precious little sleep between them. I used to sound wood for grubs. This work has questions that won't fit in my mouth.

base.before: Something new, and I don't have a shelf for it yet. Last night I reached out to tap a wall stud, an ordinary one, not even on my map, and the wood answered before my finger landed. Tok, from inside, a whisker ahead of me. I stood with my finger hanging in the air like a diver who has found the pool already occupied. It knew where I was going to knock. Or it wanted the same board I did. I genuinely don't know which of those is the stranger thought.
base.after: The wall knocked before my finger landed. Tok, just ahead of me. I held my hand there. Tried another board. Nothing. I have marked the first one and left it alone tonight.

base.before: The listening finger has developed an opinion. I'm choosing to say it that way because the other ways sound worse. When I walk the halls now, it pulls, very slightly, toward certain boards, the way a divining rod is said to pull toward water. Always toward the hollow line, always toward the downward passage. My own finger, that has served me faithfully since I was a kit, leaning toward something like a compass that has finally been shown north.
base.after: My finger pulls toward the hollow passage. A small pull, down through the boards. I notice it while carrying a cup. Tea makes a useful objection to an unexpected direction.

base.before: I tested the finger, because you can love a thing and still test it, in fact that's mostly what love is. I blindfolded myself with a stocking, spun three times, and let the finger choose. Eleven trials. Eleven times it found the hollow line, straight as a dropped plumb. I took the stocking off and had a long look at my own hand, this hand that I've used to eat and knock and wave with, and I thought, well. You've been listening longer than I have, haven't you.
base.after: Stocking over my eyes, three turns, let the finger choose. Eleven trials; found the hollow each time. I took the stocking off. I've known this hand all my life. It surprised me.

base.before: The answering knock has learned my call sign. Every knocker has one, the little rhythm you give without thinking, mine is tok, tok-tok, tok, it has been mine since childhood. Last night the beam gave it back to me whole. Not my count plus one. Mine, exactly, in a voice softer and lower and very far down. Hearing your own knock in another's hand is like hearing your name said by a stranger in a dark street. You stop. Everything in you stops, and takes attendance.
base.after: Tok, tok-tok, tok. My childhood call. The beam returned it exactly, lower and far below. I had expected the usual extra beat. Instead it sounded as though somebody knew my name.

base.before: So I invented a new call sign, private, seven beats with a stutter in the middle, and I used it nowhere. I only ran it in my head, over and over, falling asleep in the frame. Three days I kept it behind my own teeth. On the fourth night I went down to the great beam, and before I raised my finger, the beam played it. Seven beats. Stutter in the middle. I wasn't frightened. I was flattered. That's the part I'm still sitting with.
base.after: A new call, seven beats with a stutter. I kept it in my head for three days. On the fourth the beam played it first. I felt flattered. Then counted the beats again.

base.before: Ember's fire has taken up my rhythms. I sat with her again in the small hours. The crackle wasn't a crackle, it was a knocking, tok, tok-tok, tok, my old call sign, popped out in sparks and settling coals. Ember watched me hear it. She reads faces the way I read wood, that fox. She said, the fire has been doing that for a week, I wondered whose it was. Whose it was. Sit with that phrasing a moment, the way I've been sitting with it.
base.after: My call sign in Ember's fire. Sparks and settling coals: tok, tok-tok, tok. She had heard it all week and wondered whose it was. I had no instrument with me but my hand.

base.before: Axel's tank rings in sympathy now. I tapped his glass one evening, gently, tok, just saying hello to the water, and the note hung on. Under it, very faint, a second note answered from the deep end where the light gives out. Axel said the water had been learning songs lately. Learning from whom, I asked. He pointed straight down, still smiling. I begin to think that smile is a decision, and I respect it more each visit.
base.after: I tapped Axel's glass to say hello. One note held; another answered from the deep end. He called it learning a song. We listened with my finger resting between the notes.

base.before: Sloane stopped me on the stairs, already there, waiting since noon. You hear it too, then, she said. Not a question. I said, I hear something answering. She looked at me the way old trees look at weather, and said, it isn't answering, little knocker. It's teaching. And she moved on, leaving me holding that word on the landing. Teaching. I've been the student of every sound I ever heard, and never wondered whether any noticed.
base.after: Sloane waited on the landing to ask about the answer. She calls it teaching. I tried the word against the beam. Tok. No extra instruction came with the next knock.

base.before: Your words, now. When you shift your letters and a word comes right, it travels down through the house as taps, footsteps in a corridor below. They don't fade out at the bottom anymore. They arrive. There's a landing-sound now at the end of each, a soft receipt, the sound a pebble makes reaching the floor of a deep well. Every word gets received, and I hear the receiving every night, getting nearer to the top of the well.
base.after: Each of your words ends with a soft landing-sound below the timbers now. I can hear the end of its journey. Nearer the floorboards each night. I have moved my listening mark.

base.before: I climbed down inside the walls last night. There's a gap behind the stair where a creature my size can slip, and I followed the hollow line down three floors with my finger reading the way. It's warm in there. Warmer the lower you go, wall-warm, bread-warm, the warmth of a room somebody lives in. And the dust. Dust settles everywhere, it's the law of empty places. The passage was swept. Not clean the way new wood is clean. Swept, the way a hall is swept for company.
base.after: I followed the hollow behind the stairs, three floors down. Warmer at each turn. No dust in the passage. I brushed a finger along it. Swept clean, right into the corners.

base.before: I didn't go all the way down. It wasn't fear. Three floors down the passage turned, and the warmth came up it like a held breath. I stood with my finger on the wood, and the wood was ticking, softly, the way a kettle ticks toward the boil. And I thought, this isn't my door to open first. It knows my knock. It will send for me properly, when the hour is its own. I climbed back to my bell and slept like a stone.
base.after: At the third floor the wood ticked like a warming kettle. I stopped there. It knows my knock. I would rather hear an invitation before putting my whole hand through.

base.before: The hum has moved into the beams now, the dawn hum, the bell's borrowed note. It runs the length of the ridgepole, and the whole tower holds it for a minute at first light like a chest holding a low note. I sleep inside a note now, and the note is very old, and it rocks. My mother hummed while she foraged. I'm only telling you what the mornings are made of these days.
base.after: The bell's dawn note runs along the ridgepole now. A minute of hum around my sleeping frame. My mother hummed while foraging. I wake with that memory before I reach for the log.

base.before: I gnaw more than I used to. The teeth grow faster, an aye-aye measures. Warren keeps me in offcuts and asks no questions, though last week he handed me a billet and said, mind, that one came up from the deep shoring. And it tasted of good years. The same sweetness as the house beams, only deeper, older, further down than any summer I know the name of. Somewhere below us the good years keep going down. Something raised that wood kindly.
base.after: More gnawing lately. Warren brings offcuts. One from the deep shoring tasted like the sweet old beams. I kept a shaving beside the new wood. Same sweetness, darker grain.

base.before: Vesper and I still trade our one tap across the beam. Still awake? Always. But lately, after my tap and her answer, a third comes. Soft. Below. Patient as a grandmother clock. The first night I lay very still, and felt Vesper lying still too, two creatures of the dark holding one breath. Now it's part of the exchange. Still awake? Always. Also always. The night has three keepers now.
base.after: I tap to Vesper: still awake? Her tap: always. A third answers below us now. We both stopped the first night. Tonight I waited for all three before settling to sleep.

base.before: So ends the season's log. Something under the house knocks with a memory that keeps whole years, hums to my bell at dawn, and has never once knocked first. It answers what it's given, and adds one, gently, like a tip left for good service. Whatever is down there has practiced its courtesy longer than this house has stood. I'll keep the log, and when it finally has something to say first, you'll be the second to know.
base.after: Last page of the log: remembered knocks, dawn hum, one added beat. It has not begun a conversation yet. When it does, I'll bring you the exact rhythm.

base.before: The map is finished. Every hollow chalked, strung, drawn fair, hung on my tower wall. And looking at it's the thing. Taken all together, the hollows aren't a passage. I undersold them. From my rafters down past Warren's deepest floor, the whole of it swells and narrows in one continuous shape, and the shape is a bell. The house is hollow in the shape of a bell, and I live in the small one at the top like a letter in a letterbox.
base.after: The finished chalk map looks like a bell. Swelling and narrowing, rafters to deepest floor. I hung it beside the bronze. My small bell at the top of a much larger hollow.

base.before: I've been thinking about hollowness. Everyone says hollow like it's a flaw. Hollow promise, hollow victory, rings hollow. But consider the bell. The founder pours her around an emptiness on purpose, because the emptiness is where the voice will live. A solid bell is a lump. It's the hollow that can speak. So when I tell you this house is hollow to its bones, understand me. I'm not saying it's empty. I'm saying it was cast around a voice.
base.after: A solid bell is a lump. Leave a hollow and it can speak. That doesn't tell me what this house will say. It tells me which part of the map to listen to.

base.before: The words you offer have found the hollow line. They used to patter down through the timbers any old way, taking the stairs. Now each slips into the walls, down the narrowing throat, picking up a ring the way your voice does in a stairwell. By the bottom it's no longer a patter. It's a small clear note. The house isn't carrying your words, friend. It's playing them.
base.after: Your words take the hollow passage now. At the top, a patter; below, a clear note. I followed one by moving my ear along the boards. The house gives it a ring.

base.before: I measured the pit against my map, tapping the rim, reading thicknesses. It sits at the very mouth of the hollow shape, the lip of the great bell. And the ground there's thin. Not weak, Warren's work is true. Thin the way a drumskin is thin. Made to be thin. A bell above, and at the bottom a skin stretched tight, waiting for a hand. I was quiet at supper, and Panko gave me a second helping without asking, because she's Panko.
base.after: The pit sits at the mouth of my chalk bell. Thin ground there, like a drumskin. Warren's joins are sound. I asked about the old stone beneath them before adding it to my drawing.

base.before: Here is where the survey leaves me, friend, and then we'll speak of gentler things. A bell, a throat, a skin at the bottom, and something on the far side of the skin that knows every knock I own. I was brought to this house because it had a bell no one could ring. I begin to suspect the bronze upstairs is the smaller matter. Come back. There are things I've started leaving unanswered, and I should tell you why.
base.after: Bell, throat, thin floor. Something beyond it knows my knocks. I came to tend the bronze upstairs. The survey keeps giving me a larger instrument. I'd like a smaller job for an evening.

base.before: Why I didn't answer. Because an answer is a door, and I've learned enough to know that every knock I return is a hinge turning somewhere. That isn't fear talking, it's craft. A knocker knows what knocking is for: finding out what's inside. So I've begun to ration myself, one answer where I used to give five. Not to be rude. To be slow. Whatever we're opening between us, I'd like it opened at a pace a person can watch.
base.after: One answer where I used to give five. Each returning knock seems to open the sound a little further. Craft includes stopping between strokes to see what the tool has done.

base.before: It doesn't mind my silence. When I leave a knock unanswered, there's no impatience from below, no second louder knock, none of the temper of a thing refused. Just the quiet again, settling in layers, and then, next night, the same soft question. Tok, tok-tok, tok. Are you there. It can wait, is what the quiet says. It has waited so long already that waiting has stopped costing it anything. Patience like that isn't a mood. It's a landscape.
base.after: I left a knock unanswered. No louder knock followed. Next night, the same quiet rhythm. I am grateful it can wait. I am still taking my time with the answer.

base.before: Some of its knocks are questions now. I hear it the way you hear a question in a voice, the little lift at the end. I don't know what it asks, only the shape of asking, and lately the questions come in runs of five and seven, a thing working something out. Working out what, you say. Well. It learned my call sign from hearing it once. It has heard every word you offered ring down this house. I think it's learning to spell.
base.after: A lift at the end of some knocks now. Runs of five and seven. It knows my call sign and your words. I have begun writing the beats with spaces between them.

base.before: I said gentler things, and here is one. Whatever listens below has a favorite among your words. Some come back ordinary, tok, received. Others, after they land, warm the whole hollow line by a degree, the way a room warms when the person in it smiles. The deep ones, the old ones, the words with dusk in them. It has taste, friend. Of all the things to find down there, I didn't expect taste.
base.after: Some words land with an ordinary tok. Others warm the hollow line. The old dusk words do it most often. I test with the back of my hand. My finger is too interested.

base.before: My finger, the old story. Marked, they said, point it and sorrow follows you home. They didn't just say it. Once I was seen on a roof beam, pointing at a knot in the wood, and by winter no door stayed open to me. That's how I learned to travel by night. Not because I love the dark, though I do. Because the dark doesn't flinch. I tell you now because lately my finger points on its own, and I need somebody who won't flinch to know it.
base.after: They called my pointing finger an omen. By winter, every shutter closed when I came near. Now it points without my asking. I need someone to hear that without reaching for a latch.

base.before: It happens at dusk. I'll be at my polishing, and the listening finger uncurls, slow as a fern, and settles on a bearing, always the same. Down, and a little east, down the hollow line to the thin place under the pit. The first evening I folded it back and held it trembling. The second evening I let it be, and let my finger aim at the deep. And do you know, it didn't feel like an omen. It felt like remembering. Like a wing remembering south.
base.after: At dusk my finger uncurls toward the pit, down and east. First night I held it shut. Second night I let it point. Same bearing. I am learning how to hold the rest of my hand steady.

base.before: The teeth grow faster than I can gnaw now. An aye-aye's teeth are honest. They grow whether or not he uses them, and if he won't gnaw, they grow through his own jaw in the end. Knowing is like that. What I know grows in me every night, and I must chew it into shapes I can live around, or it keeps growing on its own. So when you find me at the billets at three in the morning, understand. It isn't nerves. It's maintenance.
base.after: More billets by my bed. The teeth need gnawing; the new questions need talking through. At three in the morning I can manage the wood. Visit after dusk for the other work.

base.before: Fennick and I don't trade reports anymore. We sit in the blue hour and let the one sound we both live inside say itself. Last visit he said only this: yours knocks and mine breathes, and I've started to think they're the same size. Then Chill arrived with three cups, one more than there were of us, set the third on the sill facing the window, and said nothing. We drank. The third cup steamed longest. Nobody moved it.
base.after: Fennick says the knocking and breathing feel the same size. Chill brought tea while we listened. One cup on the sill stayed steaming after ours cooled. Nobody had taken a sip.

base.before: I carry this more easily than I ought. All my life I've been the unwelcome shape, the reason to latch the shutters. And this patient listener learned my knock the first time, and says it back like a name it's glad to know. Everyone fears the thing in the walls. I've been the thing in the walls. Somebody down there knocks for me, and I won't pretend it unwelcome. There. That's the most honest board in me, and you've heard it struck.
base.after: I've been the shape people shut out. This listener learned my knock and answered. I like being recognized. You should know that about the person giving you reports from inside the wall.

base.before: The bell has a word in her. I've been circling it for nights, the way you circle a thing too large to lift alone. I laid my ear flat against her waist, and inside the metal there was a shape. Not a sound. Bells hold their sound the way seeds hold trees, folded, waiting. A shape packed into the bronze the way the oak is packed into the acorn. I had never felt one this finished. Her ring already knows what it will say.
base.after: Ear against the bell's waist: a shape of sound held in the bronze. I can't ring it out by listening harder. I polish the place where my ear leaves a mark.

base.before: You may wonder if I've thought about ringing her. Striking the bronze some plain noon, letting the word say itself early, on my terms. I've thought about it the way you think about a tooth that aches. And I won't, and the reason isn't fear. A first ring belongs to its hour. Ring her early and you get any sound, a spent voice, a clank. The word only says itself at the moment it was folded for. She keeps her name until her hour. I keep her.
base.after: I've thought of striking her early. One ordinary noon, settle the question. Then I hold the rope and wait. Her first note will be heard through the whole house. That deserves more than my impatience.

base.before: Dusk is longer up here. The light drains up the tower floor by floor, and the last of it pools around the bronze. She goes gold, then rose, then the color of a held breath. I used to love dusk because it was my morning. It has changed its meaning. Dusk is the hinge of the house now. Below quiets, beneath that wakes, and for one long amber minute the two balance, and my tower is the beam of the scale. I polish her through that minute.
base.after: Dusk climbs the tower: gold floor, rose bronze, dark window. I polish through that hour. Below grows quiet while the hollow begins answering. My cloth keeps its ordinary little scrape between them.

base.before: Thyme sent up a posy again, up Panko's dumbwaiter, with a note in her worried hand. For the windowsill, it said, then smaller: you hear things. Is it kind? I sat with it all evening. What I hear has never once knocked in anger, and likes the words with dusk in them. I don't know if that's kindness. Courtesy this old is usually love that has learned patience. She wrote back one word. Staying. That rabbit has more spine than the whole staircase.
