base.after: Thyme sent flowers and a question: is it kind? I wrote that it knocks gently, which isn't enough to know. She sent back staying. I kept her note beside the flowers.

base.before: The last leaf of the log. The house is a bell, the pit is her skin, my bronze is her echo cast small. Under it a listener with perfect memory and old taste, who has begun to knock first. I keep the tower, ration my answers, gnaw my knowing into livable shapes, and at dusk let my finger point where it will. I'm not afraid, and no longer claim that as a virtue; fear was never my note. I sleep best on the nights you offer well.
base.after: End of the log. Bell-shaped house, answering hollow, and now the first knock comes from below. I ration my replies. The blank page is ready. I won't fill it before the next sound.

base.before: I wrote the knocked letters down, with a shaking hand. I won't tell you what they spell. Not to keep it from you, but the word wasn't sent to me, and a listener with any craft knows the difference between overhearing and receiving. It went up, along the hollow line into the bronze, and my bell drank it the way dry ground drinks rain. The word in her isn't folded so tightly now. She sits differently in the frame. Heavier. No. Riper.
base.after: The knocked letters travelled up into the bronze. I wrote their rhythm with a shaking hand. The bell sits heavier in her frame now. I checked the bolts before wondering about the word.

base.before: We share a code now, the deep and I. It knocks in letters, and I know letters. There's no honest way for two speakers of one language to sit on either side of a wall forever saying nothing. So, small things. It knocks the old dusk words it loved. I knock back the weather, the frost on the sill, the smell of Panko's bread in the shaft. Neighbors, friend. I'm neighbors with what's under the world.
base.after: It knocks old dusk words. I answer with weather, frost, the smell of bread in the shaft. Small talk through a wall. I used to wish for a neighbor who would try that.

base.before: It asked about you. Among the letter-knocks came the rhythm of your words, not any one, the gait of them walking down the beams. It played your gait, then held the question-beat after. Who is that. I sat with my finger curled shut, then knocked the only true thing I had. Tok: a friend. Tok tok: a friend who keeps coming back. The warmth that came up lasted until morning, and I'm past apologizing for the sleeping.
base.after: It tapped the rhythm of your words, then a question-beat. I answered friend. A friend who returns. Warmth came up until morning. I hope friend carried the meaning I put into my hand.

base.before: I'd rather name what I've become than have you name it going down. I'm the wall between the house and what's under it, and the wall has learned to talk, and talking walls serve two rooms. Every exchange planes me thinner, translucent as a shaving, and one evening the knocking won't need me. What then, I ask, in the dark. Then it speaks for itself, and you go back to being the one who loved the sound first. There are worse retirements.
base.after: Every exchange makes the wall feel thinner. Perhaps one night it won't need my knock to speak. I'll still know which beams are sound. I am keeping the tools for that work.

base.before: I know what the bell is for. It came to me whole. All this time I thought her one ring would be a warning. The tower, the bronze raised over the whole house, everything about a bell says beware. But you don't fold a word that patient, that warm, that fond of dusk, into a warning. She isn't a warning, friend. She's a welcome. The house cast its whole hollow self around one syllable of greeting, and I'm the one who keeps the door.
base.after: I thought her first ring would warn the house. The note forming in her sounds like a welcome. I want to ring it. I am keeping that want separate from the rope.

base.before: There's an hour. I don't know its date, but I know, bone-deep, that it exists, the way you know a train by the rail beginning to sing. Everything points one way, and pointing is my inheritance. The word ripening in the bronze. The skin under the pit going tight as a drumhead. The letters rising nearer the surface each week. Somewhere ahead there's an hour with a bell in it, and all the rest of my nights are the rope being braided.
base.after: The bronze holds a word. The floor beneath the pit answers tighter. My finger keeps finding both. There is an hour approaching. I can braid a sound rope without pretending I know its date.

base.before: Understand what the rope isn't. It isn't eagerness. I haven't moved one hour toward the hour; the hour keeps itself. The rope is craft, and craft is how my kind prays. When the moment comes, the shame isn't in the doing, the shame is in fumbling it. Her ring won't be marred by a bad rope or a slipped grip. I practice the pull on a sandbag rigged at the same height. Every dusk, twelve pulls. My shoulders ache like a bellringer's already.
base.after: Twelve practice pulls at dusk, sandbag at the bell's height. A rope should hold without slipping. My shoulders ache. The practice makes my hand ready; it doesn't decide when I use it.

base.before: You've been quiet on these visits lately. You keep offering. Word after word, down the throat, onto the skin, and you've heard enough from me by now to half-know what the words are fattening. And still you keep climbing my stairs. I don't think that's foolishness. I think you're like me. You've heard the sound under everything, and it didn't sound like an ending to you either. Stay for the dusk. It's better with two.
base.after: You still climb the stairs after hearing my reports. I'd like to take that for agreement. I haven't asked. Stay through dusk if you want. There is room to tell me I'm wrong.

base.before: The finger doesn't wait for dusk anymore. It points through my sleep. I wake at midday, the long finger aimed down and east, at the thin place, steady as a roof nail. This week, a new thing. When the ridge loses the sun, it lifts. Off the deep bearing and up, through the bell mouth at the sky, as if what it points to had two addresses. I've stopped folding it in. I won't fold away my truest part because strangers made a story of it.
base.after: My finger points through sleep now, down and east. At sunset it lifts toward the sky through the bell. Two addresses. I drew both and tied a reminder to rest my hand.

base.before: It pointed back. Last night, the knocking stopped mid-run, and the whole hollow line went quiet, an attending quiet. Through the boards, a pressure of attention settled on my chest, precise as a fingertip, exactly where a point would land. It lasted three heartbeats, then resumed, softer. I laughed once at the size of the joke. Thirty years the pointer. One night, the pointed-at. Nothing in me flinched. Nothing in me wanted to.
base.after: The knocking paused. A pressure settled on my chest, exact as a fingertip, for three heartbeats. Thirty years pointing; one night pointed at. I laughed before I could choose another sound.

base.before: One more, the deepest board I own. When it found me, what it rested on was the hollow in me. Every creature has one, the gap behind the heartwood, the room nothing has ever lived in. Mine has been empty so long it had become just my note. The sound Tock makes. And the attention rested on the emptiest joist of me, and didn't recoil, didn't pity. It approved. As if to say: good. You kept it hollow. That's where the voice will go.
base.after: The attention found the empty place I carry. No recoil, no pity. I wanted to call it welcome. I rested my hand there afterward and tried to hear what was still my own.

base.before: The house is arranging itself by ear, and I seem to be taking the roll. Each keeper settles onto their own note like choristers finding pitch. Warren's spade has stopped, and his palms have started, flat on the deep stone. Ember's fire has gone steady as a held tone. Panko's kitchen rings in one key from matins to midnight. A house full of separate lives has begun to tune. Nobody called a note. The note called them.
base.after: Spade quiet, palms on stone. Fire steady, kitchen in one key. Separate sounds beginning to tune together. I tap an ordinary loose board between them. It still has its own note.

base.before: Fennick stood in my tower, ears full, and conducted the house. There, the water. There, the fire. Your beam is the pulse, and under it all, breathing at the bottom, the long note we don't name at parties. Then, what he came to say. Tock, it isn't many sounds anymore. It's one sound. And a sound that large isn't an event, it's a voice, and a voice that ready is going to want a bell. He looked at my rope. Neither of us touched it.
base.after: Fennick pointed out water, fire, beam-pulse. One sound, he said, large enough to want a bell. We looked at the rope. Neither paw nor ear can answer for the hand that pulls.

base.before: Warren came up. Warren in my tower, blinking in the height like a man on a ship. He said, I've been thinking about your question. What stops my knock on the way back. And he set his palm flat on my high floor and said: nothing stops it. It isn't stopped, it's received, and receiving takes a moment, and I mistook the moment for a thief. Then he put his cap on, said, your rope is well braided, and went back down. From Warren, that was a psalm.
base.after: Warren thinks his late knock is being received, not stopped. He tapped my floor to show me. Before leaving he checked the rope and called it well braided. I kept that part too.

base.before: Thyme keeps her promise. Staying, she wrote. This week she stayed through it. She watched my finger find the sky, ears back, paws folded like someone holding their own hands for company. After, she said, it's like watching a flower turn. I thought it would be like watching a weapon. Then, smaller: I'm so tired of being surprised that things are gentle. I gave the posy back, still sweet. Some letters should be returned with interest.
base.after: Thyme stayed while my finger turned skyward. She had expected a weapon. I showed her the knuckle, the ordinary bend of it. We put her flowers on the sill together.

base.before: Axel and I've worked out that we live at either end of the same instrument. We proved it, no striking. I hummed against her waist, just breath, and four floors down his tank dimpled in rings. Then he pressed his small hand flat to his glass, and up here my bell warmed under my ear by one soft degree. We're the two mouths of it, he said, unafraid, the way he is. The house breathes in at the water and will breathe out at the bell.
base.after: I hummed against the bronze; Axel saw rings in his tank. His paw on the glass warmed the bell under my ear. We repeated it. Two ends of one instrument, and both of us listening.

base.before: Sloane was in my tower when I woke, at the rope, the pale strand. She said, in that voice that arrives like weather: I watched a bell tower stand empty here before your grandmother's grandmother gnawed her first branch. It was never empty. It was reserved. Then she touched the rope once, the way you touch the shoulder of someone about to do a hard thing, and began her long way down the stairs. I brought her tea at the third landing.
base.after: Sloane remembers the tower before my family. She called it reserved. I looked at my fresh rope against the old beam. On her way down I brought tea to the third landing.

base.before: So the house is tuned, the table extended, the rope braided and blessed, and you're in every margin of it, your words the pulse of it. Do something for me on the nights you offer. When a word comes right, hold still one extra breath before you let it go, so it goes down warm from the holding. The received ones ring rounder. It's a small craft, the kind I can teach. It may be the last small thing either of us gets to practice.
base.after: Try holding a word one breath before offering it. I hear a rounder note when it lands. A small listening experiment, if you like. You needn't change your hands on my account.

base.before: The hollows are filling with warmth. Not closing, the passage is as open as ever. But the old cellar-cold is gone, floor by floor, replaced by bread-warmth rising from below like slow water in a lock. I climbed inside the wall one last time and hung in the dark, in the middle of the house's warm hollow body. It was like being carried in something. I haven't been carried since I was a kit. I stayed an hour.
base.after: The wall passage is warm floor by floor. Still open. I climbed inside and rested there awhile. It felt like being carried. After an hour I took myself back to the tower.

base.before: You're frightened, and that's right, and I wouldn't take it from you. I was frightened once myself, for one whole season. I can tell you what waits on the far side of a fear you carry all the way through. It looks like this branch on an ordinary evening, with the frogs singing and nothing changed but you. You're closer to that evening than you think.
base.after: Fear took a whole season of mine once. The frogs kept singing through it. I won't promise you my ending. I can share the branch while you find yours.

base.before: The center of the garden is my bowl. I want to be accurate about this, because I've been avoiding being accurate about it for a week. The beds lean toward the bowl. The place where I call from. My garden has started facing my voice, or facing what answers it, and I haven't yet worked out which, and the two aren't the same size.
base.after: The beds lean toward my calling bowl. I moved a pot to check. Same lean. I can't yet tell whether they're facing my voice or the answer beneath it.

base.before: Archimedes found my family in one of his books, imagine that, kakapo in a book older than the hills I hatched behind. He read me the passage. It said we were called the mossbirds, and that our calling was a summons across the green, in the old sense of summons. He asked what the old sense was. I didn't know. He didn't either. Neither of us liked not knowing the same thing at the same time.
base.after: Archimedes found mossbirds in an old book, calling across the green. It used the word summons. We both wanted to know who was supposed to answer. The page offered no name.

base.before: Warren says the ground under the house runs warm now, and he asked, since I know roots, whether roots could carry warmth like that. I told him the truth. Roots carry word, not warmth. Whatever is warm down there's warm the way a body is warm. He nodded slowly and said that was what the dirt had told him too, and that he had been hoping the dirt was wrong.
base.after: Warren asked whether roots could account for the warmth below. I couldn't account for that much. We compared a handful from each place. He took both back down to the lamp.

base.before: Tock's knocking has changed its pattern. It used to wander the beams, testing here, testing there, the way you tap a wall looking for the stud. Now it goes in rounds, the same route every night, and my seedlings tick along with it like a bed of little clocks. When the round passes under my garden the leaning gets briefly deeper. I've measured it. I measure everything now. It's that kind of season.
base.after: Tock's rounds pass under the beds each night. The seedlings tick along. When the knocks reach the bowl, they lean further. I tied thread to a stem so I could check tomorrow.

base.before: There are three of the stranger plants now, and they've come up in a curve, evenly spaced, the way I space things when I'm being careful. Somebody is being careful. I sat by them all night with my chin on the bed frame, watching. They grew the whole time, slow and sure of themselves, like they knew I was watching and didn't mind.
base.after: Three new plants in an even curve. The spacing is as careful as mine. I watched with my chin on the bed frame. Someone has left me very little thinning to do.

base.before: I froze again yesterday, mid-morning, one foot up. But here is the thing worth telling. There was no hawk. Nothing overhead but blue. My body called a stillness on its own, the deep old stillness we keep for when something large is passing. I stood there twenty minutes under an empty sky. I trust my body, friend. Something large was passing. The sky just didn't have it yet.
base.after: I froze with one foot up. Empty blue sky, no hawk I could see. Twenty minutes before I put it down. The watering can waited beside me. I finished that row first.

base.before: I told Bamboo about the answer under the hills. They were quiet a while, and then they said, the smoke leans, the stalks lean, and now the beds lean. We keepers of high places notice it first because we're nearest the direction things lean toward. I said my beds lean down, toward the bowl, toward the house. Bamboo smiled and said, yes. Nearest that direction too.
base.after: Bamboo's stalks lean inward; my beds lean toward the bowl. They came to see the difference. We crouched by one stem until the tea cooled. Looking took longer than the explanation.

base.before: I lay in the middle bed last night, looking up as I do. For a moment the stars felt less like a garden I could never reach and more like a lid. A friendly lid, mind. But a lid knows something a sky doesn't, which is what it's covering. I'm going to sit with that thought a while. Don't carry it down the stairs with you. It's a roof thought. It lives up here.
base.after: Lying in the middle bed, I thought the stars looked like a lid. I usually call them a garden. Same lights tonight, a less comfortable name. I moved to the fern corner.

base.before: The mast diary again. My grandmother's rule was, when the slate fills before the season turns, dig your bowl deeper. I always took that for old-bird nonsense, the way half of inherited wisdom is. The slate filled this morning, three weeks before the turn. I stood over my bowl a long time with my digging foot ready. I haven't deepened it yet. I want to want to. That isn't the same as wanting to.
base.after: Grandmother said to deepen the bowl when the mast slate filled early. Three weeks early today. I stood with my digging foot ready. Then put it down. An old instruction can wait one evening.

base.before: You're part of this, you know. I say it gladly, not gravely, so put your shoulders down. The warm lines in my soil are your words, the early rows are your rows, half this out-of-season plenty has your hand in it somewhere. My garden knew you before I did. I'm only saying that if this is a mast year coming, you're one of the trees that agreed.
base.after: Your words warm the lines beneath my beds. Half this early growth follows their arrival. I am glad of the fruit. I should ask what the warmth means before thanking you for all of it.

base.before: I deepened the bowl. Last night, in the end, by moon, with both feet, the old way. I'll tell you exactly what it felt like, because you of all creatures should know. It felt like answering a letter I'd been pretending not to have opened. The garden was very quiet while I dug. Approving-quiet. The beds leaned in like family at a christening.
base.after: I deepened the bowl by moonlight. Both feet, the old way. The beds were quiet while I worked. I left the loose soil in a pile beside it. I may want to fill some back.

base.before: The answer has started coming before I call. I sat in the deepened bowl, filling with air, and the note rose under the hills while my chest was still rising. It knows the call is coming, the way the beds know rain. I let my air out slowly, uncalled. There didn't seem to be any need. We're past introductions, whatever we are.
base.after: I filled my chest to call. The answer began before I had let the air out. I sat through its note in silence. Then tried one small boom of my own.

base.before: Axel sent word up through the house that the water has been showing him a green place, high up, full of moonlight, and did I know it. Friend, he has never climbed to my garden. He described the bowl. He described the stranger plants, veins and all. I sent back one word, yes, because the alternative was a great many words and none of them fit in Panko's dumbwaiter.
base.after: Axel described moonlit beds, a bowl, the new plants' veins. He has never climbed here. I sent back a leaf to compare. It was the shape his water had shown him.

base.before: Sleep well tonight. The moon is fat, the beds are leaning, the bowl is deep, and far under the hills the answer hums like a neighbor humming in another room. I find I'm not frightened, and I've decided to trust that the way I trust my own held breath. Come up again soon. The garden asks after you when you're gone. I've stopped pretending that it doesn't.
base.after: Full moon, deep bowl, a hum beneath the beds. I sleep well up here. Visit again when you can. Bring an account from downstairs; my garden has been keeping most of my attention.

base.before: I've been thinking about where a call goes when nobody answers it. Ninety years of booms, out across the valleys, and I always pictured them thinning into nothing, the way ripples do. But ripples don't thin into nothing. They arrive somewhere, smaller and smaller, and something very patient could stand at the far edge of the water and collect them. All of them. In order.
base.after: Ninety years of unanswered calls. I used to imagine them fading away. Now I wonder whether something kept them. I'd like to hear one young call again. I might not recognize my voice.

base.before: The mast has begun. I can say it plainly now, no diary needed. Every tree this valley owns is setting fruit at once, in the wrong month, under a sun that never agreed to it. In the old forest a mast year meant one thing. It's time. The trees have decided, root to root, and everything that waited on them may now stop waiting.
base.after: Fruit setting across the valley, all at once, in the wrong month. In the old forest that meant a mast year. I have brought out the largest baskets. They may still be too small.

base.before: But a mast year is a decision, and I keep returning to that word with my head tipped. The trees decide together, and nobody has ever caught them deciding. Something under the forest carries the agreement. I used to find that cozy, the ground busy with cooperation. Now I stand on this roof, over a warm and busy house, and I wonder who proposed.
base.after: A mast year brings everything into fruit together. I used to enjoy the agreement without wondering how it began. Up here, over the warm house, I have begun looking beneath the beds.

base.before: I asked Sloane, because she's the only one whose answers arrive slower than my questions. I said, in your long life, who decides a mast year. She thought about it for the better part of a day, and then she said, the ones who are ready feed the ones who decide. After that I didn't want the rest of the answer, and she gave me the mercy of not finishing it.
base.after: Sloane took most of a day over my mast-year question. She says the ready ones feed the ones who decide. I went back to the beds and counted who was being fed.

base.before: I counted what my garden feeds. The moths go down to the house. The warm lines come up from your words. The fruit is swelling for something that hasn't arrived. A garden is always for someone, friend, that's the first law, deeper than the weed law. I planted every bed of this one. I'm no longer certain I chose the someone.
base.after: Moths go down; warmth comes up; fruit swells for something not here yet. I planted every bed. I would like to meet the creature my garden has begun feeding.

base.before: And still, and still. I walk the rows at moonrise and the beds are beautiful past anything I ever grew alone, heavy and glad and leaning. My whole chest fills up the old way, air and call and no room left over. If this is being used, it has the exact weather of being needed. I've decided to keep walking the rows while I think. A gardener can think and water at the same time. It's mostly what we do.
base.after: The beds are more beautiful than anything I grew alone. Being used feels remarkably like being needed from here. I can water while I think about the difference. The plants still need water.

base.before: The bowl holds sound now. I dropped a pebble in yesterday, testing the depth. The little knock of it went round and round the sides, down and down, longer than any bowl of dirt should keep a sound. When it finally faded I heard, very faint, underneath, the answer-note rise slightly. The way you shift in your chair when the visitor you're expecting rattles the gate.
base.after: Dropped a pebble into the bowl. Its knock circled much longer than a little bowl of dirt should allow. Under the fading sound, the answer rose. I hadn't meant the pebble as a call.

base.before: I sleep in the bowl now. I want to say it before someone tells you and it arrives sounding stranger than it is. The fern corner got cold, and the bowl is warm, blood-warm, all night, and a kakapo sleeps where the warmth is, that's older than every custom I own. I dream down there. Green dreams. Deep ones. I wake with soil in the folds of me and no memory of digging.
base.after: The fern corner is cold; the bowl stays warm. I sleep there now. Green dreams, soil in my feathers by morning. I put a stone at the edge to mark how deep it is.

base.before: The fruit is nearly ripe and nothing is eating it. That's wrong, friend, that's deeply wrong, fruit is a payment and the whole world usually queues up. The birds land, look, and leave it. The moths circle it and go down to the house instead. Everything that lives here has agreed the fruit is spoken for. I never heard the speaking. I just keep the orchard.
base.after: Ripe fruit, no takers. Birds land and leave it. Moths pass by. Usually I have to defend a basket from half the valley. Tonight I offered one fruit from my own foot. Still nothing.

base.before: I tried an experiment I'm not proud of. I took one fruit, the ripest, from the nearest stranger plant, and I hid it, in a seed tin, under the north bed frame. By morning the tin stood open on the middle of the path with the fruit set on top of it, unbruised, facing the bowl. Nothing about it was angry. That's what I keep telling myself. It was the patience of a thing correcting a child's sum.
base.after: I hid a ripe fruit in a tin under the north bed. Morning: tin open on the path, fruit on top, facing the bowl. Unbruised. I wish that detail were more reassuring.

base.before: I've stopped calling the strangers strangers. They came up in my beds, they drink my watering, they flower on my old hours. They're mine, whatever else they also are, the way this house is ours, whatever else it also is. You may hear how much work that sentence is doing. It's bearing what I ask it to bear. We're all carrying something up here.
base.after: I have stopped calling the new plants strangers. I water them; they grow in my beds. I still don't know what brought them. Naming something mine doesn't answer where it came from.

base.before: Vesper watches the sky and I watch the ground, and lately at the gate post we compare, and the accounts have begun to match. Vesper says the stars over this house sit lower. I say the ground under this garden listens closer. Same lean, opposite shores. Whatever is coming, it's coming from both directions at once, which is to say, it isn't coming. It's closing.
base.after: Vesper says the stars sit lower. I feel the warmth nearer my roots. We compare at the gate post. Her chart and my planting slate are beginning to need the same margin.

base.before: Come up again soon. The mast is at its heaviest, the bowl keeps its warmth, and I find the nights are better with company that has hands. There's more to say and I'm nearly ready to say it. A gardener knows almost to the day when a thing will be ready. For the garden's sake I hope I'm wrong by a season. I have never once been wrong by a season.
base.after: The mast is heavy. The bowl stays warm. Come sit while I sort the baskets. I know when fruit is nearly ready. This season I would appreciate being a little wrong.

base.before: The others speak of an arrangement now, downstairs, in the new plain way everyone has taken up. Archimedes has it from his books, Ember from her fire. I have it from the green, which doesn't read and doesn't burn but has been in this longer than either. The arrangement is a mast year, friend. That's the whole of it. Every tree agreeing at once, and every creature that waited being told, it's time. Only the forest is bigger than I thought. The forest was never trees.
base.after: Archimedes calls it an arrangement. I recognize a mast year's plenty, arriving together. But this reaches beyond the trees. I have kept an empty basket beside the full ones. Plenty must go somewhere.

base.before: The fruit has begun to fall, and it falls wrong, and I've stopped flinching at the word wrong. It falls slowly. Each one comes off its branch and takes a long moment getting to the ground, the way a leaf does, except these are heavy as eggs. The garden hands its fruit down, friend. Nothing here drops anything anymore. It's all giving, all the way down the branch.
base.after: Fruit leaves the branch and falls slowly, heavy as an egg but drifting like a leaf. I put a basket under one and waited. For once I didn't have to hurry the catch.

base.before: I gathered the fallen fruit and carried it, bed by bed, to the rim of the bowl, because there was nowhere else it wanted to go. A gardener past a certain point simply cooperates with where things want to go. By midnight the rim was ringed all the way round. By morning the fruit was gone, and the soil where it sat was the warmest my feet have ever stood on. My feet have stood on ninety years of summers.
base.after: I carried the fallen fruit to the bowl. A complete ring by midnight. Gone by morning, warm soil where it had rested. I brought up the empty baskets and counted them twice.

base.before: Tock came up in the dark and knocked once on my gate post, and the bowl answered before I could. One knock, one deep note, quick as talk. Tock listened the way Tock listens, head aside, and said, hollow all the way down, and it has never sounded hollow before. Hollow is what a thing sounds like when what fills it has moved closer to the opening. Then Tock thanked my garden, not me, and went back down. I stood with my foot on the post a long while after that.
base.after: Tock knocked on the gate post. The bowl answered first. He listened with his head tipped, then sounded the wood again. I kept one foot on the post. The note reached it from below.

base.before: Ember climbed to my garden for the first time, all that way, fur full of woodsmoke, and stood at the bowl a long time. She said, I read fire, and this is a fire, the slowest one I have ever been shown. Green flame, hundred-year wood. Then she asked what it was burning toward, and I said, the same thing yours is, and she laughed her quick laugh. Neither of us said the rest, because the rest was standing under the ground listening, and it seemed rude to introduce it before it was ready.
base.after: Ember called the bowl a slow green fire. I showed her where the fruit had gone. We sat with our feet on the warm soil. My garden and her grate needed a new conversation.

base.before: Bamboo and I keep the two open places, their attic and my open beds, the passing room and the no-room-at-all. We've begun taking tea together at the roof gap, they on the ladder, me among the beans. Last night they said, what comes will pass my window on its way to your garden. I said, then wave, and Bamboo smiled the long smile and said, I intend to bow. We didn't clink cups. It wasn't that kind of toast. It was better.
base.after: Bamboo and I take tea at the roof gap, ladder on one side, beans on the other. They expect a visitor above us. I asked them to tell me if it bends the bean poles.

base.before: The stranger plants have grown taller than me, and they've turned, friend. All of them, in one night, a quarter turn, the way a congregation turns when the doors open at the back. They face the bowl. Everything in this garden now faces the bowl, the beds, the fruit trees, the moths' road, the plants, and lately, I notice, the gardener. I didn't turn. I was turned. There's a difference, and I've stopped needing the difference to comfort me.
base.after: Plants taller than me now. All turned toward the bowl in one night. I found myself facing it too. I went to weed the east bed, where the work needs me to look elsewhere.

base.before: I want to tell you about your words, because you bring them and you deserve the accounting. They come up through my soil as warmth, I told you that in the bright season. Here is what I didn't know then. Warmth in soil is a message in the oldest post there's, root to root, the mast post, the one the trees agree through. Your words have been voting, friend. Every one of them, warm and sure, down there with the roots, saying, time, time, time. The mast didn't happen to us. We asked for it. You and I asked most.
base.after: Your words warmed the roots and helped bring the mast. I tended what grew. We helped something happen before either of us knew what it was. A grower has to account for that too.

base.before: Warren asked me what the roots want, since I speak root. I told him, roots only ever want one thing, to hold what stands and feed what comes. He said, that's what foundations want, word for word. We looked at each other a long moment, the digger and the planter, and then he said, well, and went back down. I've thought about that well ever since. There's a whole sermon in a wombat's well.
base.after: Warren's foundations hold what's above; my roots feed what comes. We sat at the bed edge comparing the work. He asked what we'd braced it for. I had been hoping he knew.

base.before: The bowl sang on its own last night. No pebble, no boom, no knock from below. One long note out of the bare earth, low and full and patient, and every bed leaned in by a finger's width. The fruit on the rim of the dark went bright for the length of it, like windows when a lamp goes past inside the house. I didn't join in. Not yet. A caller knows his cue, friend, and that note wasn't the duet. That note was the tuning.
base.after: The bare bowl sang. No pebble, no call from me. The beds leaned while the note lasted. I kept my chest quiet and listened until it ended. My answering breath could wait.

base.before: You keep offering words below, and I keep planting above. Between us the house hums like a hive with one bee too many, or one flower too few, I can't decide which. Come up soon. The last fruit is loosening. I can hear it deciding, the little tick of the stem letting go one fiber at a time. When it goes I don't want the garden to be empty of everyone but me. Some hours are load-bearing, friend. That one will want both of us under it.
base.after: The last fruit is loosening. A small tick at the stem each night. Come up if you can. I would like company when it falls, and another pair of feet to carry the basket.

base.before: The last fruit fell at moonrise, and it fell like the others, slowly, handed down. The garden went silent the way the hill used to go silent before my own voice broke it. And then, friend, the bowl breathed. Once. In. I felt the air move over my feathers toward the earth. Everything I have, every year, every call, every bed, sat still inside me and attended. There was no out-breath. It's holding it. Somewhere under this house, everything is holding it, and the welcome is in my chest like held air. I'm keeping both, breath and welcome, until they're called for.
base.after: The last fruit came down at moonrise. Then the bowl drew air over my feathers, one long inward breath. No breath out. I waited with my feet in the soil. The empty basket stayed beside me.

coordinated.before: The fire has been spelling one word all night, friend, the same word over and over in the embers. I laughed at first, because what else do you do. It is still spelling it. Have you noticed it too?
coordinated.after: One word in the embers all night. I laughed and stirred the fire. Same word when it settled. One of yours, friend. Come close enough to read it with me.

coordinated.before: I found a passage in the oldest text that references a word I have been meeting in my dreams. Your word. One of the ones you brought. I have checked the dating twice, and the book is older than both of us.
coordinated.after: Your word appears in the oldest text. I checked the date twice, then the binding. The book predates your visit. That is what I can establish.

coordinated.before: The stew made itself this morning. I mean that plainly: the pot was already going when I reached it, and the recipe was the letters you arranged, in order. I just followed along, the way you follow a guest's wishes.
coordinated.after: The pot was simmering before I reached the kitchen. Your letters lay in the recipe's order. I tasted it before adding anything. Somebody has learned my method.

coordinated.before: The water is writing something on the inside of the glass, over and over, the same shapes tracing themselves and fading and tracing themselves again, and here is the thing, friend, they are your shapes, the ones you bring, I would know them anywhere.
coordinated.after: Your letters on the inside of the glass! I wipe them away and the water draws them again. Same crooked little shapes. I wish it would try a fish.

coordinated.before: I keep writing the same word in my notes. Over and over, margin after margin. I do not remember doing it, which for me is a serious filing incident. My hand simply moves. The word is one of yours.
coordinated.after: Your word, every margin. My handwriting. No recollection of the entries. I have clipped the pages together and put my pen in another room.

coordinated.before: There is a word in the wind now, and it repeats without resting. I have listened from every side of the camp to be certain. You must have heard it too. Everyone must have heard it by now.
coordinated.after: One word in the wind. Repeats without a breath. I took bearings from each side of camp. Did you hear it? I need an answer besides my own.

coordinated.before: Does the house feel warmer to you, friend? Not cozy warm, I know cozy, cozy is my whole profession. This is different. This is the warmth of something holding its breath before a happy surprise. I keep saying happy. Help me keep saying it.
coordinated.after: The den is warmer. I opened the window and blamed the fire. Still warm with the grate dark. I would like it to be a pleasant surprise. That's a wish, friend.

coordinated.before: The walls have been humming. Very faintly, at the edge of measurement, like a struck tuning fork three rooms away. It began, by my notes, just after the last words you brought.
coordinated.after: The walls hum after each arrangement. Faint, but my tuning fork catches it. I've entered the times beside your visits. The columns match so far.

coordinated.before: My pots rattle now whenever your words are offered, a little shiver along the whole shelf, all of them at once. I used to blame the stove. I have checked the stove. It is not the stove.
coordinated.after: Your words arrive and every pot rattles. I tightened the shelf, checked the stove, moved a saucepan to the floor. The saucepan rattled there too.

coordinated.before: The water in my tank rose overnight, a whole knuckle higher, and no one added a drop, I asked everyone, I even asked twice politely, so the new water came from somewhere else, and I keep wondering what it left behind to be here.
coordinated.after: The water rose a knuckle overnight! Nobody added any. I asked twice. I marked the glass this morning. My line looks terribly small beside all that water.

coordinated.before: The ground's got a gentle vibration to it now, steady, rhythmic, like machinery running somewhere too deep to name. Started right after the last words you brought. I've had my palm flat on the floor half the night. It doesn't stop.
coordinated.after: Steady vibration under the boards. Started after your last words. I've checked the braces. Sound timber, tight joins. Whatever's running is below my work.

coordinated.before: The garden is growing faster than it should, much faster, and I would know, I measure. And there are dark flowers coming up along the warm strip, whole rows of them, velvet-dark and very sure of themselves. I did not plant those. I want that written down somewhere. I did not plant those.
coordinated.after: Three new rows along the warm strip. Dark flowers. I didn't plant them. I have the seed packets and the bed plan. Please put those beside what you see.

coordinated.before: The walls sing after you offer your words now. One low note, held longer than any breath could hold it, sitting just underneath everything else I hear. It is getting louder, and I measure it every night, and I am telling you because someone besides my ears should know.
coordinated.after: The walls hold one low note after your words. Longer each night. I time it by the kettle, which is still behaving like a kettle. That matters to the measurement.

coordinated.before: The branches hum after your words are offered, a vibration that comes up through the bark and settles into my bones. I have hung in this tree through storms and seasons, and the tree has never once hummed for weather. It hums for you.
coordinated.after: The branch hums after your words arrive. I know its storm noises. This is new. Gerald has moved out of the fur against the bark. A second opinion.

coordinated.before: I dreamed of a shape last night, friend. It was burning in my fireplace like it had always lived there, like it was the landlord and the fire was the tenant. I woke up smiling, and then I sat very still about the smiling. Did you dream it too?
coordinated.after: A shape in my fireplace, in the dream. I woke smiling and began laying two cups. Caught myself at the second. Did you dream a visitor too?

coordinated.before: We all had the same dream. I have confirmed it methodically, animal by animal, the same shape, the same feeling of being courteously observed. A whole house of sleepers, one dream. There is no citation for that. I looked.
coordinated.after: Same shape in every dream I have collected. I kept the accounts separate until each was written. They agree. I have no independent sleeper outside the house to ask.

coordinated.before: When I woke, the shape was in my water, the very one from the dream, hanging there patient as a moon, and I understood all at once that it had not followed me out of the dream, the dream had been it letting me visit.
coordinated.after: The dream shape was in the water when I woke. I waved. It waited. Perhaps I'd been visiting its dream! I would like to ask whose turn it was.

coordinated.before: I dreamed last night, for the first time in years. My sleep has been an empty green room for decades, and something walked into it and stood where I could see it. Something old is waking up, and it wanted even the slowest of us to know.
coordinated.after: First dream in years. A visitor in the clearing where my sleep usually does nothing. I was sorry to wake. I have written that down before telling you the rest.

coordinated.before: In the deepest sitting, I saw the shape from the dream. It is beautiful, the way a mountain is beautiful, without needing anyone's permission. And it knows we are watching. It has always known. Being watched is how it opens.
coordinated.after: I saw the dream shape while sitting awake. Beautiful. I kept wanting the beauty to settle my next question. I moved my cushion and looked again.

coordinated.before: I heard the shape before I saw it, there in the dream. It was not silent at all. It has a sound it has been saving, and it was waiting, very patiently, for all of us to lie down and listen at the same time.
coordinated.after: I heard the shape before I saw it. Same note as the walls, with a gap at the end. I woke waiting for the gap to finish.

otherSceneAndContinuity.before: Light shows the rail. An unlit lantern gives me the valley.
otherSceneAndContinuity.after: I shade the lantern to watch the valley. Brightness isn't always help.

otherSceneAndContinuity.before: Tock laid his chalk map over my tunnel drawings, his hollows above, my galleries below, and the two lines nested like a tongue in a groove. Thirty years I dug my half of that shape without knowing it had another half. He knew inside a season. That aye-aye reads a house the way I read ground. I'll tell you what I told him: between his ceiling and my floor, there's nothing left in this building we haven't heard.
otherSceneAndContinuity.after: Tock laid his chalk map over my tunnel drawings, his hollows above, my galleries below, and the two lines nested like a tongue in a groove. I braced my half of that shape without knowing it had another half. He knew inside a season. That aye-aye reads a house the way I read ground. I'll tell you what I told him: between his ceiling and my floor, there's nothing left in this building we haven't heard.

otherSceneAndContinuity.before: The lantern remains unlit. I still like the valley better than the porch.
otherSceneAndContinuity.after: I shade the lantern when I want the valley. The porch can wait.

otherSceneAndContinuity.before: I called that peace. I should have asked whether everyone could still disagree with me.
otherSceneAndContinuity.after: I moved my cushion out of the middle. There is room to sit somewhere else. I should have left it sooner.

otherSceneAndContinuity.before: A good door works from both sides. I can build the frame. I cannot decide who passes through.
otherSceneAndContinuity.after: I'll hang a door you can open from either side. You try the latch before I call it finished.

otherSceneAndContinuity.before:
A note passes through the timber.
No voice is asked to drown another.
otherSceneAndContinuity.after:
A note passes through the timber.
A spoon taps a cup. The small sound still carries.
